4538.prule: Fixed final (sesquisyllabic template): the Pearic word is a single stressed main syllable, optionally preceded by one weakly stressed presyllable whose nucleus is a neutral /ə/; the stressed syllable is therefore always the last, and the source allows no word longer than two syllables. Weight plays no role (the presyllable is stressless by template, not by weight).

4540.heavy: long syllable = (C)VV (sec. 2.4, p. 27: 'Syllables are either long or short. A short syllable has the shape (C)V. A long syllable has the shape (C)VV.'); long vowels are analysed as VV sequences in close transition (pp. 10-12, 24-25). Codas do not exist.
4540.dflt: penultimate syllable of the phonological phrase (penultimate voiced syllable in final phrases)
4540.prule: Stress is not phonemic. One phrase stress per phonological phrase (the stretch between final juncture /#/ and non-final juncture //): on the last syllable of the phrase if it is long ((C)VV), otherwise on the penultimate syllable; in final phrases only voiced syllables count, since a short vowel before final juncture is frequently devoiced. Any other position marks contrastive emphasis. No word-level stress rule is stated; non-final words in a phrase carry no phrase stress (e.g. [#kua+noho+ia+ki+te+táane//]).
4540.srule: Yasuda's 'syllable stress' (non-primary prominence): every syllable is stressed except a short (C)V syllable immediately before any juncture (/#/, // or +); among stressed syllables a long (C)VV syllable is louder than a short one, and /a/ louder than /e o/, louder than /i u/. A graded prominence over the juncture-bounded stretch, not an alternating or word-level secondary stress; no rhythmic secondary stress is described.

The grammar's ch. 2 summary phrases the same fact as 'main stress falls on the final or the penultimate syllable of the lexical root' with the pitch accent on one mora of that syllable. Minimal pairs by accent position/mora (káti 'saddle' vs katí 'how many?', čúur/čuúr, séeti/seetí). No computable fixed position: the source says placement 'is not entirely predictable' and 'must be defined as lexical'.

4547.tone: Three lexical tones /55/ /33/ /31/ (Burling & Phom 1998 pp. 19-20; Bano 2008 §5.10 pp. 168-171 'In Phom language, tones are phonemic... There are three register tones in Phom'; Phom 2018 acoustic confirmation, three tones, 'It was observed that tone sandhi is not present in Phom', ch. 5 p. 110). Glottal-final syllables show no tonal contrast. Neither 'stress' nor 'accent' as a prosodic property of Phom occurs in Burling & Phom (full-text search of the scanned scan: only 'strongly accented' in an English-vowel comparison p. 16 and 'accents over the vowels' as a tone-marking remark p. 21). Bano 2008 lists 'Stress' only as a Chomsky-Halle prosodic feature category (§5.9.3 p. 165) never applied to Phom, plus 'final unstressed vowel schwa' in an apocope rule (p. 185); her tone-placement remark (p. 168): 'In bi-syllabic and tri-syllabic words, the high tones are usually marked on the second syllable, but if the second syllable is followed by a glottal stop, the tone is marked on the first syllables of the words.' Phom 2018 names 'the effect of the stress plays on the tone' as an objective (ch. 5 p. 104) but reports no finding; one offhand line: consonant clusters in derived words 'are pronounced with the same amount of stress as different syllables' (ch. 1 §1.6 p. 30). 4549.heavy: Placement of strong stress is quantity-insensitive (always final); syllable structure governs only the degree of non-final prominence (full CV(C)ᵀ = weakly stressed vs. short open CVᵀ presyllable = unstressed) and the fact that a CVᵀ syllable never bears strong stress, which the source states as the restriction 'with all types of syllabic structure except CVᵀ' (i.e. CVᵀ presyllables do not occur word-finally).
4549.prule: Strong (primary) stress falls on the last syllable of every word; monosyllables carry it on their only syllable. Non-contrastive and fully predictable (no stress mark written). Patterns listed: disyllables US, WS; trisyllables WUS, WWS; quadrisyllables UWUS, UWWS, WWWS, all ending in S.
4549.srule: Non-final syllables carry one of two lesser degrees, determined by syllable structure, not by position: a full syllable CV(C)ᵀ (open or closed, with tone) is weakly stressed (W, marked ˌ); a short open presyllable CVᵀ (tone 2 or 3, e.g. ka-, ta-, sa-, la-) is unstressed (U). Either may occupy the first or the penultimate position (§3.3.2, p. 70). No positional or rhythmic secondary stress is described.
4549.quote: Stress is defined as loudness and duration. In this study, stress is predictable from its position in a word and from the syllabic structure. Accordingly, no stress mark is written in phonemic transcription. The strongly stressed syllable (with all types of syllabic structure except CVᵀ) always occupies the last position, and the weakly stressed syllable (with syllabic structure CV(:)(C)ᵀ) and the unstressed syllable (with syllabic structure CVᵀ) precede the strongly stressed syllable in the poly-syllabic words. [p. 57] ... Word stress in Phuan can be mentioned in four types: in monosyllabic …

4549.tone: Phuan is tonal: every syllable in Eam-eium's transcription carries a numbered tone superscript (values 1-9 appear on the pages read, e.g. ha:⁶ 'to give', ɲok⁹ 'to raise', ka² 'presyllable'). Stress is described as a separate, predictable positional property (loudness and duration) alongside tone; the unstressed CVᵀ presyllables still carry a tone (T2,3). The source does not treat tone and stress as interacting beyond this.

Patterns: US, WS; WUS, WWS; UWUS, UWWS, WWWS (three degrees S/W/U; words of 1-4 syllables).

Donnelly says it is only 'superficially clear that Phuthi lacks stressed syllables' and analyses prominence as 'composite, distributed and paradigm-sensitive': a right-aligned syllabic trochee at the word edge (ALIGN-WD-RT, RHTYPE=T, STRESS-TO-WEIGHT) whose head, the penult, is 'the stressed position' and is made heavy, but that redundant penult length surfaces only in phrase-final (declarative) words and is revoked phrase-medially; lexical H tone is repelled from the long penult (AVOID_PROMINENCE) and aligns to the antepenult phrase-finally, to the penult phrase-medially, and to penult or ultima in grammatical paradigms. The prominence position is thus defined by tone alignment and phrase-final length, not by a single quantity-insensitive word-stress position.
4552.srule: None: Donnelly posits 'a single, right-aligned, binary stress foot' headed by the (phrase-final) penult and states that 'the language has an ‘incomplete’ metrical system: there is no evidence for further footedness in the language beyond this cluster of phenomena within the last three syllables of the word' (no iterative footing, hence no rhythmic/secondary stresses; the term 'secondary stress' itself is not used).

4557.dq: Apart from word stress, sentence intonation may also apply to some words such that they are pronounced with a higher pitch (see chapter 8 for details on sentence types). This is typified for instance with the focusing particles nao and ya.
4557.dloc: Beimers 2008, §3.9.2.3 'Focus particle Intonation', p. 56 (first sentence of the subsection, directly after §3.9.2.2 Stress on p. 55)
4557.prule: Word stress is lexically determined and not predictable from syllable count or weight: each word keeps stress on the syllable that bore it in its etymon (English or a Solomons vernacular), and the stressed syllable retains stress even when epenthesis (klaem ~ kalaem) or word-final paragoge (skul ~ sukulu) adds syllables; stress is never contrastive. Beimers explicitly treats the earlier fixed-penultimate (Bugotu 1972:27) and fixed-initial (Simons & Young 1978:18) accounts as partial truths subsumed by the lexical account.
4557.srule: Not mentioned in Beimers 2008 (section 3.9.2.2 'Stress', pp. 54-56 read in full; whole text consulted): the grammar places only the single word stress and says nothing about secondary or rhythmic stresses.
4557.quote: Various analyses of Pijin have provided different accounts of the stress pattern of Pijin words. Bugotu (1972, p.27) says “Stress in Pidgin English, as is true in most Melanesian native tongues, usually falls on the penultimate syllable.” The account by Simons and Young (1978, p.18) says that “stress normally falls on the first syllable of Pijin words (although there are, of course, a few exceptions).” In saying that, they allow that epenthetic vowels in consonant clusters do not cause stress to shift to any new first syllable created by epenthesis. It seems that both positions express part o…

4557.exq_: Of course for words that occur neither in the substrate vernaculars nor in English (e.g. yufala ‘you PL’) the only part of this account that is relevant is that stress is lexically determined.
4557.tone: No tone. §3.9.2.3 'Focus particle Intonation' describes higher pitch on focus particles nao and ya and rising pitch on the final word of interrogatives as sentence intonation, explicitly 'apart from word stress'.

4558.prule: Word stress on the penultimate syllable of polysyllabic content words (Costello 2014); in Bradley 1970's terms the microstress falls on the tonic syllable of the microsegment, i.e. the first syllable of the bisyllabic couplet, which is always followed by exactly one posttonic syllable; pretonic syllables (prefixes) precede it (/ka'hoo/ 'box', /ma'we?e/ 'this particular house'). Monosyllables and a few bisyllabic function words are unstressed.
4558.srule: None within the word: Costello 2014 (sec. 3.2, p. 25) mentions no secondary stress, and Bradley 1970 (sec. 1.25 p. 13, 1.4 p. 17, 1.5 pp. 19-21) gives each microsegment (couplet) a single microstress with atonic pre- and postmicrosegment syllables; his second degree, macrostress, is the phrase (macrosegment) peak and 'falls on the syllable of a microsegment that in other environments bears merely the microstress' (p. 20).

4560.prule: Stress is an intensity accent riding on the HIGH level of a three-level (H/M/L), non-contrastive pitch pattern whose shape is 'casi predecible' from syllable count: disyllables H-L = stress on the first syllable (kinship terms L-H = final, 28 of 32 terms); trisyllables M-H-L = stress on the second syllable (H-H-L 'de muy baja frecuencia'); four-syllable words one of three patterns (M-H-M-L, H-H-H-L, M-H-H-L) with 'un acento primario y uno secundario, o dos acentos primarios' and no single position; five-syllable words (mostly compounds) 'siempre' two primary stresses, on the second syllable and the penult ('excepto unos pocos nombres que lo llevan en la última'). Occasionally stress falls on a final low-toned syllable. Suffixation moves the H/stress one syllable to the right (['júkɨ] 'árbol' → [jū'kɨgɨ]). quantity-insensitive: syllables are (C)V. Grids the source fixes: 2σ 10, 3σ 010, 5σ 01010 (two primaries); 4σ not fixed.
4560.srule: Exists, placement not given: four-syllable words may have 'un acento primario y uno secundario, o dos acentos primarios'; the source does not say which syllable carries the secondary. 4560.tone: Three pitch levels (alto, medio, bajo; muy alto/muy bajo by position in the intonation contour). The author finds no distinctive function at any level ('no le hemos hallado valor fonológico en ningún nivel de la lengua', p. 382), judges that 'el pisamira no sea una lengua tonal' (p. 382) and excludes tone from the phonemic transcription (p. 383), while noting that cognates differ from Bará/Tatuyo/Tucano only by tone pattern (Cuadro 3). Stress is the intensity correlate of the H level. Tone and stress 'varían de posición también en forma arbitraria' in CVV words and in vowel sequences with /a/ (p. 383). Later work reported second-hand in Rodríguez Preciado 2018 (§2.5, pp. 35-36): Valderrama 2014 finds tone patterns depend on syllable count and stress always falls on the H syllable 'pero no deja clara la función fonológica'; Gómez-Imbert 2011a p. 1451 groups Pisamira with Tuyuca/Desano/Siriano/Yurutí as having one H mora per word, i.e. a culminative pitch-accent analysis is possible; Rodríguez Preciado herself (p. 155) says she could corroborate tonal distinctions empirically but does not analyse them.

4563.prule: Lexical tone, four tonemes on the major syllable (T1 low falling creaky/glottalised, T2 mid delayed-falling modal, T3 mid level breathy with optional brief final /h/, T4 short high checked with oral or glottal stop coda). No word-stress rule is stated for Phong; the only stress remark is the group-level one that the sesquisyllabic presyllable (prefix or reduced first morpheme of a compound) is toneless and unstressed, i.e. prominence sits on the tone-bearing major (final) syllable.

4563.exq_: The same applies to most Tangsa-Nocte varieties. The presyllable is toneless and unstressed
4563.tone: Phong is described as a four-tone language following the general Tangsa-Nocte tone categorisation (p. 234; Table 9.1 p. 235): T1 low falling with creak/glottalisation (not limited to open syllables), T2 mid delayed-falling modal, T3 mid level breathy (breathiness 'almost prevalent enough as to be considered a primary feature of the toneme', p. 235), T4 'short, high and checked' (p. 239). Some lexemes have shifted category relative to cognates ('head' /kʰu3/ vs T2 elsewhere; 'stamping' /nak4/ vs T1 elsewhere). Tone sandhi: complete regressive neutralisation of a T1/T2 first syllable of a bisyllabic compound to a mid-level T3-like contour ('leech' /si3 vət4/ < /si1/ 'blood'); T3 final aspiration elided non-finally. Stress: the thesis says nothing Phong-specific; at group level (sec. 5.1.3 p. 94; repeated p. 171 'sesquisyllabic causative prefix... by definition toneless and unstressed' and Fig. 7.9 caption 'sesquisyllabic prefixes... are unstressed and atonal') the presyllable is toneless and unstressed and is marked tone 0 (Phong example /i0 ma1/ 'scar', p. 235). The intonation discussion elsewhere in the thesis notes emphasis 'happens through lengthening and stress' at utterance level; that is not a word-stress rule.
